voiceover.text: So, why do endurance athletes train mostly easy? Here's a club runner with five hours a week, who wants a faster ten kilometres. Races hurt, they reason, so every session should hurt too. All five runs are as hard as they can go. Predict what happens over eight weeks, and write down two reasons why. Then write what you'd change.

scenes.title: two thresholds bound the aerobic zone

voiceover.text: Aerobic training has a floor and a ceiling. Below the aerobic training threshold, roughly seventy per cent of maximum heart rate, the stimulus is usually too small to keep improving the fitness of someone who already trains. Above the lactate threshold, around eighty-five to ninety per cent of maximum heart rate in trained athletes, lactate and hydrogen ions build up faster than they're cleared, so the effort can't last. That's the same point as Year 11's seventy to eighty per cent of maximum aerobic capacity, just measured by heart rate. Above it is the anaerobic work from last time. Between them is the aerobic zone, about seventy to eighty-five per cent of maximum heart rate, a little higher in trained athletes. The lower part, seventy to eighty per cent, can be held for a long time, so it builds volume. The upper part, near the threshold, is a strong stimulus to raise the threshold itself, but it's tiring. These percentages are rules of thumb, and the thresholds move as an athlete adapts. Raising the lactate threshold lets an athlete race at a higher share of the ceiling they already have.

All four aerobic methods arrange the same work differently. Continuous training is steady effort with no rest and no planned change of pace, usually twenty to ninety minutes in the lower zone. It builds volume safely, but it's monotonous, and it doesn't match sports whose pace keeps changing. Fartlek, Swedish for speed play, is continuous too, but the pace varies without a fixed plan, with surges chosen by the athlete or the terrain. It trains changes of pace, but its load is hard to record. Aerobic interval training uses set work bouts and set recoveries, inside the zone, like five four-minute efforts just below the threshold. Unlike HIIT, the work is longer and a little easier, and the rests are shorter than the work. It piles up time at an intensity you couldn't hold continuously, but it's tiring, so one or two a week. Circuit training is a sequence of stations, so the exercise changes rather than the pace. It's aerobic only if heart rate stays up. Load it heavily with full rests, and it becomes resistance training.

Now the hook. Many endurance adaptations depend on the total time spent training aerobically: more capillaries around the muscle, more and bigger mitochondria, more aerobic enzymes, more blood plasma, and a bigger stroke volume. To pile up that much time, most of it has to be at an intensity you can repeat tomorrow. Some work does need to sit near the threshold, because raising it means working close to it. But do that every day, and three things happen. Total volume falls, because you can't recover. The hard sessions get worse, because you're doing them tired. And the risk of injury and illness rises. So our runner improves at first, then stalls. Swap to about three easy runs and two hard ones, and the same five hours work better. Easy training isn't laziness. It's what makes the hard training possible.

Use the routine from last time: demand profile, matched method, trade-off. A marathon is one long, steady effort, so mostly continuous running, with intervals to lift the threshold. But continuous work alone leaves you unpractised at surging. A soccer midfielder moves all game with unpredictable surges, so fartlek, plus intervals. The catch is that fartlek is hard to measure across a squad. A two-thousand-metre rower races well above the threshold, close to maximum aerobic capacity, so aerobic intervals near and above it, limited by their cost. And sprint sports need an aerobic base too. They're anaerobic in the effort, but aerobic in the recovery. Refilling phosphocreatine and clearing by-products between efforts both depend on the aerobic system. So no method is best. The sport's pattern and the time of year decide.

Aerobic training is the base, but it has limits. It doesn't build top speed or power, so a team player trained only aerobically is slow over the first ten metres. Lots of aerobic work alongside heavy lifting can blunt strength gains, so the two are usually kept apart in the week. And a big aerobic score is a capacity, not a performance. Skill and tactics are trained separately.
Two things to remember. Continuous holds pace, fartlek varies it freely, intervals vary it by plan, and circuits vary the exercise. And easy training makes hard training possible.

Two exam questions. First. An AFL umpire runs about twelve kilometres a game at constantly changing speeds and tires in the last quarter. And a fifty-year-old's easy thirty-minute jog has felt the same for a year. For each, choose an aerobic method, justify it, and state one trade-off. Pause here to answer.

The umpire suits fartlek, because it trains changing speeds across a long game. The trade-off is that the load is hard to record. The jogger has adapted to the same easy stimulus, so add one interval session a week just below the threshold. The trade-off is fatigue, so build it slowly. The classic mistake is more of the same easy jogging.

Second. A coach runs SIT for rugby league forwards with a poor aerobic base: six-second sprints with only thirty seconds of rest. Predict what happens to sprint power across the set, and explain why. Pause here to answer.

Sprint power falls across the set. Thirty seconds can't refill phosphocreatine, and refilling depends on the aerobic system, so a poor base refills it even more slowly. By-products build up too. So the session stops training peak power. Lengthen the rests, and build the base. The classic mistake is treating the energy systems as switches.

So keep most aerobic work easy, put a little near the threshold, and match the method to the sport's pattern. But energy supply isn't the whole story. Three more method families train range, strength and skill. How do flexibility, strength and skill training differ?
